title: Outliers
author: Malcolm Gladwell

lessons.title: The Mystery of Roseto
lessons.key_idea: The surprising health of one small Pennsylvania town shows that success and wellbeing often come from community and context, not just individual choices.

lessons.title: Why Birthdays Shape Hockey Stars
lessons.key_idea: Small early advantages, like being born just after an age cutoff, snowball over time into big differences in who succeeds.

lessons.title: The Ten Thousand Hour Rule
lessons.key_idea: True mastery takes roughly 10,000 hours of practice, and the people who get there usually had rare chances to put in those hours.

lessons.title: Born at the Right Moment
lessons.key_idea: The year you are born can matter enormously, as shown by how many tech pioneers were born in the mid-1950s.
issues: scene 8: The closing scene is almost entirely text. Its only visual is a small compass icon in the top-right corner, which does not illustrate what the narration says (a big change unfolding, stepping through its door, bringing others along). The right half of the frame is mostly empty. (fix: Replace the compass with a larger illustration in the right half, for example an open amber door with a figure stepping toward it and two or three smaller figures following behind, reusing the door and person shapes from scene 7. Scale the illustration to fill roughly the right 40% of the stage.)

lessons.title: Why Genius Is Not Enough
lessons.key_idea: Beyond a certain level, a higher IQ adds little, and practical skills learned at home, like confidently asking for what you need, often decide who gets ahead.

lessons.title: The Lessons of Joe Flom
lessons.key_idea: Timing, family background and meaningful work that is complex, independent and rewards effort combined to launch an unlikely legal superstar.

lessons.title: Feuds and the Culture of Honor
lessons.key_idea: Cultural attitudes from our ancestors, like the honor code behind the feuds of Harlan, Kentucky, can shape our behavior generations later.
issues: scene 2: The pointing hand under the question points right, toward empty space, away from the Appalachian map it should connect to. (fix: Flip the hand to point left toward the row of feud markers, or remove it.)

scene 4: The herder panel is almost empty: only a moon and a lone figure. Nothing shows the flock, so the 'flock can vanish overnight' idea does not come across. (fix: Add a row of dashed or ghosted sheep outlines, or empty pen markers, beside the herder to show the missing flock.)

scene 6: The crossed-out sheep icon sits directly on top of the 'visualgrowth.app' watermark and nearly touches it, which looks crowded. (fix: Move the sheep icon left, next to the bottom statement 'They never herded sheep. The reflex stayed.', with clear spacing from the watermark.)

lessons.title: Culture in the Cockpit
lessons.key_idea: Plane crashes are often linked to cultural habits of deference, and airlines like Korean Air became safer by teaching crews to speak up directly.

lessons.title: Rice Paddies and Math Skills
lessons.key_idea: A cultural legacy of hard, patient rice farming and clear number words helps explain why many Asian students persist and excel at math.

lessons.title: Building Opportunity on Purpose
lessons.key_idea: Schools like KIPP show that if success comes from opportunity and culture, we can deliberately create the conditions that let many more people become outliers.

plan.title: Outliers
plan.author: Malcolm Gladwell
plan.confidence_note: I know this book's structure, chapters and main examples in detail, from Roseto and Canadian hockey to Korean Air and KIPP schools.
plan.one_liner: Success isn't just talent and grit. It's hidden opportunities, lucky timing and the cultures we inherit.
plan.summary: Malcolm Gladwell challenges the myth of the self-made genius. He argues that extraordinary achievers, the outliers, owe their success to more than brains and hard work. In the first half, he looks at opportunity. A birth month can decide a hockey career. Thousands of hours of practice separate experts from amateurs. Being born in the right year can open doors that stay shut for everyone else. In the second half, he turns to cultural legacy. Attitudes passed down for generations shape how we argue and how we handle risk. They even shape how pilots speak in a cockpit, and how hard students work at math. Gladwell's point is hopeful. If success comes from opportunities and environments, then we can deliberately build better ones and give far more people a real chance to excel.
